CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening headaches over the past few months.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
52-year-old male presenting for neurology consultation regarding newly diagnosed pituitary lesion. Patient reports worsening headaches that began approximately three months ago, initially 3/10 severity and now 6/10 severity. Pain is located behind the eyes described as a dull, nagging ache. Onset was gradual. Headaches tend to be worse in the morning and last a few hours at a time. Nothing makes them better or worse. Patient denies radiation of pain. Additionally reports recently bumping into door frames. Denies nausea, fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, or syncope. Denies recent changes in vision, though eyes were checked in the fall. Patient previously tried Tylenol without improvement and discontinued. Workup for headaches initiated with brain MRI and serology, during which pituitary lesion was incidentally discovered.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, syncope, nausea, or feeling sick. Denies vision changes. Reports recent clumsiness with bumping into door frames. States he does not think he has had any changes in balance. No other symptoms reported.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Patient reports past clinical history is unremarkable. Denies any medical problems.

MEDICATIONS
Patient denies taking any medications regularly. Tried Tylenol a few times for headaches but it did not work and he stopped.

ALLERGIES
Not discussed.

FAMILY HISTORY
Patient reports he was adopted and has no knowledge of family medical history.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient works as a computer programmer. Married for 25 years. Recently purchased a small house. Denies alcohol use, tobacco use, and recreational drug use. States he has never used these substances.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Patient is alert, oriented to time, place, and person. Affect is appropriate and speech is fluent. Cranial nerve examination is grossly intact. No focal motor or sensory deficit in upper or lower extremities. Visual acuity and eye movements are normal. Pupils are equal and reactive. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision is normal.

RESULTS
Laboratory studies from 3/3/21 including CBC, BMP, coagulation studies, and CRP all normal. Pituitary hormone profile demonstrates low TSH with all other results normal. Brain MRI with contrast from 3/4/21 reveals a well-defined pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles are normal in size with no other abnormalities noted.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Benign appearing pituitary adenoma with optic chiasmal compression. Patient is symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of compression. Surgical intervention via transsphenoidal approach is indicated to excise adenoma and decompress pituitary fossa. Discussed risks of surgery including anesthesia risks (heart attack, stroke, death), infection, need for further surgery, wound issues such as spinal fluid leak or infection, seizure, stroke, permanent numbness, weakness, difficulty speaking, or death. Patient will be referred to ophthalmology for full eye examination and visual field testing prior to surgery to map peripheral vision for comparison post-operatively. Patient will see surgery scheduler to arrange transsphenoidal surgery. Pathology examination will be performed on removed adenoma for definitive diagnosis.
